          n3324 text "\r\nLLM Powered Autonomous Agents\r\n"
        n3325 text "Date: June 23, 2023 | Estimated Reading Time: 31 min | Author: Lilian Weng\r\n"
        n3326 text "Table of Contents\r\n"
        n3327 text "Building agents with LLM (large language model) as its core controller is a cool concept. Several\r\nproof-of-concepts demos, such as "
        n3328 link "AutoGPT"
          n3329 text "AutoGPT"
        n3330 text ", "
        n3331 link "GPT-Engineer"
          n3332 text "GPT-Engineer"
        n3333 text " and "
        n3334 link "BabyAGI"
          n3335 text "BabyAGI"
        n3336 text ", serve as inspiring\r\nexamples. The potentiality of LLM extends beyond generating well-written copies, stories, essays\r\nand programs; it can be framed as a powerful general problem solver.\r\n"
        n3337 heading = "2"
          n3338 text "Agent System Overview\r\n"
        n3339 text "In a LLM-powered autonomous agent system, LLM functions as the agent’s brain, complemented\r\nby several key components:\r\n"
        n3340 text "Planning\r\nSubgoal and decomposition: The agent breaks down large tasks into smaller, manageable\r\nsubgoals, enabling efficient handling of complex tasks.\r\nReflection and refinement: The agent can do self-criticism and self-reflection over past\r\nactions, learn from mistakes and refine them for future steps, thereby improving the quality of\r\nfinal results.\r\n"
        n3341 text "Memory\r\nShort-term memory: I would consider all the in-context learning (See "
        n3342 link "Prompt Engineering"
          n3343 text "Prompt Engineering"
        n3344 text ") as\r\nutilizing short-term memory of the model to learn.\r\nLong-term memory: This provides the agent with the capability to retain and recall (infinite)\r\ninformation over extended periods, often by leveraging an external vector store and fast\r\nretrieval.\r\n"
        n3345 text "Tool use\r\nThe agent learns to call external APIs for extra information that is missing from the model\r\nweights (often hard to change after pre-training), including current information, code\r\nexecution capability, access to proprietary information sources and more."
        n3346 text "|\r\n"
        n3347 text "Figure 1: Overview of a LLM-powered autonomous agent system.\r\n"
        n3348 heading = "2"
          n3349 text "Component One: Planning\r\n"
        n3350 text "A complicated task usually involves many steps. An agent needs to know what they are and plan\r\nahead.\r\n"
        n3351 heading = "2"
          n3352 text "Task Decomposition\r\n"
        n3353 link "Chain of thought"
          n3354 text "Chain of thought"
        n3355 text " (CoT; "
        n3356 link "Wei et al. 2022"
          n3357 text "Wei et al. 2022"
        n3358 text ") has become a standard prompting technique for\r\nenhancing model performance on complex tasks. The model is instructed to “think step by step” to\r\nutilize more test-time computation to decompose hard tasks into smaller and simpler steps. CoT\r\ntransforms big tasks into multiple manageable tasks and shed lights into an interpretation of the\r\nmodel’s thinking process.\r\n"
        n3359 text "Tree of Thoughts ("
        n3360 link "Yao et al. 2023"
          n3361 text "Yao et al. 2023"
        n3362 text ") extends CoT by exploring multiple reasoning possibilities at\r\neach step. It first decomposes the problem into multiple thought steps and generates multiple\r\nthoughts per step, creating a tree structure. The search process can be BFS (breadth-first search)\r\nor DFS (depth-first search) with each state evaluated by a classifier (via a prompt) or majority vote.\r\n"
        n3363 text "Task decomposition can be done (1) by LLM with simple prompting like \"Steps for XYZ.\\n1.\" ,\r\n\"What are the subgoals for achieving XYZ?\" , (2) by using task-specific instructions; e.g. \"Write\r\na story outline.\" for writing a novel, or (3) with human inputs.\r\n"
        n3364 text "Another quite distinct approach, LLM+P ("
        n3365 link "Liu et al. 2023"
          n3366 text "Liu et al. 2023"
        n3367 text "), involves relying on an external classical\r\nplanner to do long-horizon planning. This approach utilizes the Planning Domain Definition\r\nLanguage (PDDL) as an intermediate interface to describe the planning problem. In this process,\r\nLLM (1) translates the problem into “Problem PDDL”, then (2) requests a classical planner to\r\ngenerate a PDDL plan based on an existing “Domain PDDL”, and finally (3) translates the PDDL plan\r\nback into natural language. Essentially, the planning step is outsourced to an external tool,"
        n3368 image "Unlabeled image"
        n3369 text "|\r\nassuming the availability of domain-specific PDDL and a suitable planner which is common in\r\ncertain robotic setups but not in many other domains.\r\n"
        n3370 heading = "2"
          n3371 text "Self-Reflection\r\n"
        n3372 text "Self-reflection is a vital aspect that allows autonomous agents to improve iteratively by refining\r\npast action decisions and correcting previous mistakes. It plays a crucial role in real-world tasks\r\nwhere trial and error are inevitable.\r\n"
        n3373 text "ReAct ("
        n3374 link "Yao et al. 2023"
          n3375 text "Yao et al. 2023"
        n3376 text ") integrates reasoning and acting within LLM by extending the action space\r\nto be a combination of task-specific discrete actions and the language space. The former enables\r\nLLM to interact with the environment (e.g. use Wikipedia search API), while the latter prompting\r\nLLM to generate reasoning traces in natural language.\r\n"
        n3377 text "The ReAct prompt template incorporates explicit steps for LLM to think, roughly formatted as:\r\n"
        n3378 text "Figure 2: Examples of reasoning trajectories for knowledge-intensive tasks\r\n(e.g. HotpotQA, FEVER) and decision-making tasks (e.g. AlfWorld Env,\r\nWebShop). (Image source: "
        n3379 link "Yao et al. 2023"
          n3380 text "Yao et al. 2023"
        n3381 text ").\r\n"
        n3382 text "In both experiments on knowledge-intensive tasks and decision-making tasks, ReAct works\r\nbetter than the Act -only baseline where Thought: … step is removed.\r\n"
        n3383 text "Reflexion ("
        n3384 link "Shinn & Labash 2023"
          n3385 text "Shinn & Labash 2023"
        n3386 text ") is a framework to equip agents with dynamic memory and self\u0002reflection capabilities to improve reasoning skills. Reflexion has a standard RL setup, in which the\r\n"
        n3387 text "Thought: ...\r\nAction: ...\r\nObservation: ...\r\n... (Repeated many times)"
        n3388 image "Unlabeled image"
        n3389 text "|\r\nreward model provides a simple binary reward and the action space follows the setup in ReAct\r\nwhere the task-specific action space is augmented with language to enable complex reasoning\r\nsteps. After each action , the agent computes a heuristic and optionally may decide to reset\r\nthe environment to start a new trial depending on the self-reflection results.\r\n"
        n3390 text "Figure 3: Illustration of the Reflexion framework. (Image source: "
        n3391 link "Shinn &"
          n3392 text "Shinn &"
        n3393 link "Labash, 2023"
          n3394 text "\r\nLabash, 2023"
        n3395 text ")\r\n"
        n3396 text "The heuristic function determines when the trajectory is inefficient or contains hallucination and\r\nshould be stopped. Inefficient planning refers to trajectories that take too long without success.\r\nHallucination is defined as encountering a sequence of consecutive identical actions that lead to\r\nthe same observation in the environment.\r\n"
        n3397 text "Self-reflection is created by showing two-shot examples to LLM and each example is a pair of\r\n(failed trajectory, ideal reflection for guiding future changes in the plan). Then reflections are added\r\ninto the agent’s working memory, up to three, to be used as context for querying LLM.\r\n"
        n3398 text "Figure 4: Experiments on AlfWorld Env and HotpotQA. Hallucination is a more\r\ncommon failure than inefficient planning in AlfWorld. (Image source: "
        n3399 link "Shinn &"
          n3400 text "Shinn &"
        n3401 link "Labash, 2023"
          n3402 text "\r\nLabash, 2023"
        n3403 text ")\r\n"
        n3404 text "at ht"

        n3407 text "|\r\nChain of Hindsight (CoH; "
        n3408 link "Liu et al. 2023"
          n3409 text "Liu et al. 2023"
        n3410 text ") encourages the model to improve on its own outputs by\r\nexplicitly presenting it with a sequence of past outputs, each annotated with feedback. Human\r\nfeedback data is a collection of , where is the prompt, each is a\r\nmodel completion, is the human rating of , and is the corresponding human-provided\r\nhindsight feedback. Assume the feedback tuples are ranked by reward, The\r\nprocess is supervised fine-tuning where the data is a sequence in the form of\r\n, where . The model is finetuned to only predict\r\nwhere conditioned on the sequence prefix, such that the model can self-reflect to produce better\r\noutput based on the feedback sequence. The model can optionally receive multiple rounds of\r\ninstructions with human annotators at test time.\r\n"
        n3411 text "To avoid overfitting, CoH adds a regularization term to maximize the log-likelihood of the pre\u0002training dataset. To avoid shortcutting and copying (because there are many common words in\r\nfeedback sequences), they randomly mask 0% - 5% of past tokens during training.\r\n"
        n3412 text "The training dataset in their experiments is a combination of "
        n3413 link "WebGPT comparisons"
          n3414 text "WebGPT comparisons"
        n3415 text ", "
        n3416 link "summarization"
          n3417 text "summarization"
        n3418 link "from human feedback"
          n3419 text "\r\nfrom human feedback"
        n3420 text " and "
        n3421 link "human preference dataset"
          n3422 text "human preference dataset"
        n3423 text ".\r\n"
        n3424 text "Figure 5: After fine-tuning with CoH, the model can follow instructions to\r\nproduce outputs with incremental improvement in a sequence. (Image source:\r\n"
        n3425 link "Liu et al. 2023"
          n3426 text "Liu et al. 2023"
        n3427 text ")\r\n"
        n3428 text "The idea of CoH is to present a history of sequentially improved outputs in context and train the\r\nmodel to take on the trend to produce better outputs. Algorithm Distillation (AD; "
        n3429 link "Laskin et al."
          n3430 text "Laskin et al."
        n3431 link "2023"
          n3432 text "\r\n2023"
        n3433 text ") applies the same idea to cross-episode trajectories in reinforcement learning tasks, where\r\nan algorithm is encapsulated in a long history-conditioned policy. Considering that an agent\r\ninteracts with the environment many times and in each episode the agent gets a little better, AD\r\nconcatenates this learning history and feeds that into the model. Hence we should expect the next\r\npredicted action to lead to better performance than previous trials. The goal is to learn the process\r\nof RL instead of training a task-specific policy itself.\r\n"
        n3434 text "Dh = {(x, yi, ri, zi)}\r\nn\r\ni=1 x yi\r\nri yi zi\r\nrn ≥ rn−1 ≥ ⋯ ≥ r1\r\n"
        n3435 text "τh = (x, zi, yi, zj\r\n, yj\r\n,…, zn, yn) ≤ i ≤ j ≤ n yn"
        n3436 image "Unlabeled image"
        n3437 text "|\r\n"
        n3438 text "Figure 6: Illustration of how Algorithm Distillation (AD) works.\r\n(Image source: "
        n3439 link "Laskin et al. 2023"
          n3440 text "Laskin et al. 2023"
        n3441 text ").\r\n"
        n3442 text "The paper hypothesizes that any algorithm that generates a set of learning histories can be distilled\r\ninto a neural network by performing behavioral cloning over actions. The history data is generated\r\nby a set of source policies, each trained for a specific task. At the training stage, during each RL\r\nrun, a random task is sampled and a subsequence of multi-episode history is used for training,\r\nsuch that the learned policy is task-agnostic.\r\n"
        n3443 text "In reality, the model has limited context window length, so episodes should be short enough to\r\nconstruct multi-episode history. Multi-episodic contexts of 2-4 episodes are necessary to learn a\r\nnear-optimal in-context RL algorithm. The emergence of in-context RL requires long enough\r\ncontext.\r\n"
        n3444 text "In comparison with three baselines, including ED (expert distillation, behavior cloning with expert\r\ntrajectories instead of learning history), source policy (used for generating trajectories for\r\ndistillation by "
        n3445 link "UCB"
          n3446 text "UCB"
        n3447 text "), RL^2 ("
        n3448 link "Duan et al. 2017"
          n3449 text "Duan et al. 2017"
        n3450 text "; used as upper bound since it needs online RL), AD\r\ndemonstrates in-context RL with performance getting close to RL^2 despite only using offline RL\r\nand learns much faster than other baselines. When conditioned on partial training history of the\r\nsource policy, AD also improves much faster than ED baseline.\r\n"
        n3451 text "Figure 7: Comparison of AD, ED, source policy and RL^2 on environments that\r\nrequire memory and exploration. Only binary reward is assigned. The source\r\npolicies are trained with "
        n3452 link "A3C"

        n3463 text "| Component Two: Memory\r\n"
        n3464 text "(Big thank you to ChatGPT for helping me draft this section. I’ve learned a lot about the human\r\nbrain and data structure for fast MIPS in my "
        n3465 link "conversations"
          n3466 text "conversations"
        n3467 text " with ChatGPT.)\r\n"
        n3468 heading = "2"
          n3469 text "Types of Memory\r\n"
        n3470 text "Memory can be defined as the processes used to acquire, store, retain, and later retrieve\r\ninformation. There are several types of memory in human brains.\r\n"
        n3471 text "1. Sensory Memory: This is the earliest stage of memory, providing the ability to retain\r\nimpressions of sensory information (visual, auditory, etc) after the original stimuli have ended.\r\nSensory memory typically only lasts for up to a few seconds. Subcategories include iconic\r\nmemory (visual), echoic memory (auditory), and haptic memory (touch).\r\n2. Short-Term Memory (STM) or Working Memory: It stores information that we are currently\r\naware of and needed to carry out complex cognitive tasks such as learning and reasoning.\r\nShort-term memory is believed to have the capacity of about 7 items ("
        n3472 link "Miller 1956"
          n3473 text "Miller 1956"
        n3474 text ") and lasts for\r\n20-30 seconds.\r\n"
        n3475 text "3. Long-Term Memory (LTM): Long-term memory can store information for a remarkably long\r\ntime, ranging from a few days to decades, with an essentially unlimited storage capacity. There\r\nare two subtypes of LTM:\r\nExplicit / declarative memory: This is memory of facts and events, and refers to those\r\nmemories that can be consciously recalled, including episodic memory (events and\r\nexperiences) and semantic memory (facts and concepts).\r\nImplicit / procedural memory: This type of memory is unconscious and involves skills and\r\nroutines that are performed automatically, like riding a bike or typing on a keyboard.\r\n"
        n3476 text "Figure 8: Categorization of human memory."
        n3477 image "Unlabeled image"
        n3478 text "|\r\nWe can roughly consider the following mappings:\r\n"
        n3479 text "Sensory memory as learning embedding representations for raw inputs, including text, image or\r\nother modalities;\r\nShort-term memory as in-context learning. It is short and finite, as it is restricted by the finite\r\ncontext window length of Transformer.\r\nLong-term memory as the external vector store that the agent can attend to at query time,\r\naccessible via fast retrieval.\r\n"
        n3480 heading = "2"
          n3481 text "Maximum Inner Product Search (MIPS)\r\n"
        n3482 text "The external memory can alleviate the restriction of finite attention span. A standard practice is to\r\nsave the embedding representation of information into a vector store database that can support\r\nfast maximum inner-product search ("
        n3483 link "MIPS"
          n3484 text "MIPS"
        n3485 text "). To optimize the retrieval speed, the common choice is\r\nthe approximate nearest neighbors (ANN) algorithm to return approximately top k nearest\r\nneighbors to trade off a little accuracy lost for a huge speedup.\r\n"
        n3486 text "A couple common choices of ANN algorithms for fast MIPS:\r\n"
        n3487 link "LSH"
          n3488 text "LSH"
        n3489 text " (Locality-Sensitive Hashing): It introduces a hashing function such that similar input items\r\nare mapped to the same buckets with high probability, where the number of buckets is much\r\nsmaller than the number of inputs.\r\n"
        n3490 link "ANNOY"
          n3491 text "ANNOY"
        n3492 text " (Approximate Nearest Neighbors Oh Yeah): The core data structure are random\r\nprojection trees, a set of binary trees where each non-leaf node represents a hyperplane\r\nsplitting the input space into half and each leaf stores one data point. Trees are built\r\nindependently and at random, so to some extent, it mimics a hashing function. ANNOY search\r\nhappens in all the trees to iteratively search through the half that is closest to the query and then\r\naggregates the results. The idea is quite related to KD tree but a lot more scalable.\r\n"
        n3493 link "HNSW"
          n3494 text "HNSW"
        n3495 text " (Hierarchical Navigable Small World): It is inspired by the idea of "
        n3496 link "small world networks"
          n3497 text "small world networks"
        n3498 text "\r\nwhere most nodes can be reached by any other nodes within a small number of steps; e.g. “six\r\ndegrees of separation” feature of social networks. HNSW builds hierarchical layers of these\r\nsmall-world graphs, where the bottom layers contain the actual data points. The layers in the\r\nmiddle create shortcuts to speed up search. When performing a search, HNSW starts from a\r\nrandom node in the top layer and navigates towards the target. When it can’t get any closer, it\r\nmoves down to the next layer, until it reaches the bottom layer. Each move in the upper layers\r\ncan potentially cover a large distance in the data space, and each move in the lower layers\r\nrefines the search quality.\r\n"
        n3499 link "FAISS"
          n3500 text "FAISS"
        n3501 text " (Facebook AI Similarity Search): It operates on the assumption that in high dimensional\r\nspace, distances between nodes follow a Gaussian distribution and thus there should exist\r\nclustering of data points. FAISS applies vector quantization by partitioning the vector space into\r\nclusters and then refining the quantization within clusters. Search first looks for cluster"
        n3502 text "|\r\ncandidates with coarse quantization and then further looks into each cluster with finer\r\nquantization.\r\n"
        n3503 link "ScaNN"
          n3504 text "ScaNN"
        n3505 text " (Scalable Nearest Neighbors): The main innovation in ScaNN is anisotropic vector\r\nquantization. It quantizes a data point to such that the inner product is as similar to\r\nthe original distance of as possible, instead of picking the closet quantization centroid\r\npoints.\r\n"
        n3506 text "Figure 9: Comparison of MIPS algorithms, measured in recall@10. (Image\r\nsource: "
        n3507 link "Google Blog, 2020"
          n3508 text "Google Blog, 2020"
        n3509 text ")\r\n"
        n3510 text "Check more MIPS algorithms and performance comparison in "
        n3511 link "ann-benchmarks.com"
          n3512 text "ann-benchmarks.com"
        n3513 text ".\r\n"
        n3514 heading = "2"
          n3515 text "Component Three: Tool Use\r\n"
        n3516 text "Tool use is a remarkable and distinguishing characteristic of human beings. We create, modify and\r\nutilize external objects to do things that go beyond our physical and cognitive limits. Equipping\r\nLLMs with external tools can significantly extend the model capabilities.\r\n"
        n3517 text "xi\r\n~xi ⟨q, xi⟩\r\n∠q, ~xi"
        n3518 image "Unlabeled image"
        n3519 text "|\r\n"
        n3520 text "Figure 10: A picture of a sea otter using rock to crack open a seashell, while\r\nfloating in the water. While some other animals can use tools, the complexity is\r\nnot comparable with humans. (Image source: "
        n3521 link "Animals using tools"
          n3522 text "Animals using tools"
        n3523 text ")\r\n"
        n3524 text "MRKL ("
        n3525 link "Karpas et al. 2022"
          n3526 text "Karpas et al. 2022"
        n3527 text "), short for “Modular Reasoning, Knowledge and Language”, is a neuro\u0002symbolic architecture for autonomous agents. A MRKL system is proposed to contain a collection\r\nof “expert” modules and the general-purpose LLM works as a router to route inquiries to the best\r\nsuitable expert module. These modules can be neural (e.g. deep learning models) or symbolic (e.g.\r\nmath calculator, currency converter, weather API).\r\n"
        n3528 text "They did an experiment on fine-tuning LLM to call a calculator, using arithmetic as a test case.\r\nTheir experiments showed that it was harder to solve verbal math problems than explicitly stated\r\nmath problems because LLMs (7B Jurassic1-large model) failed to extract the right arguments for\r\nthe basic arithmetic reliably. The results highlight when the external symbolic tools can work\r\nreliably, knowing when to and how to use the tools are crucial, determined by the LLM capability.\r\n"
        n3529 text "Both TALM (Tool Augmented Language Models; "
        n3530 link "Parisi et al. 2022"
          n3531 text "Parisi et al. 2022"
        n3532 text ") and Toolformer ("
        n3533 link "Schick et al."
          n3534 text "Schick et al."
        n3535 link "2023"
          n3536 text "\r\n2023"
        n3537 text ") fine-tune a LM to learn to use external tool APIs. The dataset is expanded based on whether\r\na newly added API call annotation can improve the quality of model outputs. See more details in the\r\n"
        n3538 link "“External APIs” section"
          n3539 text "“External APIs” section"
        n3540 text " of Prompt Engineering.\r\n"
        n3541 text "ChatGPT "
        n3542 link "Plugins"
          n3543 text "Plugins"
        n3544 text " and OpenAI API "
        n3545 link "function calling"
          n3546 text "function calling"
        n3547 text " are good examples of LLMs augmented with tool\r\nuse capability working in practice. The collection of tool APIs can be provided by other developers\r\n(as in Plugins) or self-defined (as in function calls).\r\n"
        n3548 text "HuggingGPT ("
        n3549 link "Shen et al. 2023"
          n3550 text "Shen et al. 2023"
        n3551 text ") is a framework to use ChatGPT as the task planner to select\r\nmodels available in HuggingFace platform according to the model descriptions and summarize the\r\nresponse based on the execution results."
        n3552 image "Unlabeled image"
        n3553 text "|\r\n"
        n3554 text "Figure 11: Illustration of how HuggingGPT works. (Image source: "
        n3555 link "Shen et al."
          n3556 text "Shen et al."
        n3557 link "2023"
          n3558 text "\r\n2023"
        n3559 text ")\r\n"
        n3560 text "The system comprises of 4 stages:\r\n"
        n3561 text "(1) Task planning: LLM works as the brain and parses the user requests into multiple tasks. There\r\nare four attributes associated with each task: task type, ID, dependencies, and arguments. They\r\nuse few-shot examples to guide LLM to do task parsing and planning.\r\n"
        n3562 text "Instruction:\r\n"
        n3563 text "The AI assistant can parse user input to several tasks: [{\"task\": task, \"id\",\r\ntask_id, \"dep\": dependency_task_ids, \"args\": {\"text\": text, \"image\": URL, \"audio\":\r\nURL, \"video\": URL}}]. The \"dep\" field denotes the id of the previous task which\r\ngenerates a new resource that the current task relies on. A special tag \"-task_id\"\r\nrefers to the generated text image, audio and video in the dependency task with id\r\nas task_id. The task MUST be selected from the following options: {{ Available Task\r\nList }}. There is a logical relationship between tasks, please note their order. If\r\nthe user input can't be parsed, you need to reply empty JSON. Here are several\r\ncases for your reference: {{ Demonstrations }}. The chat history is recorded as {{\r\nChat History }}. From this chat history, you can find the path of the user\u0002mentioned resources for your task planning.\r\n"
        n3564 text "(2) Model selection: LLM distributes the tasks to expert models, where the request is framed as a\r\nmultiple-choice question. LLM is presented with a list of models to choose from. Due to the limited\r\ncontext length, task type based filtration is needed.\r\n"
        n3565 text "Instruction:"
        n3566 image "Unlabeled image"
        n3567 text "| Given the user request and the call command, the AI assistant helps the user to\r\nselect a suitable model from a list of models to process the user request. The AI\r\nassistant merely outputs the model id of the most appropriate model. The output\r\nmust be in a strict JSON format: \"id\": \"id\", \"reason\": \"your detail reason for the\r\nchoice\". We have a list of models for you to choose from {{ Candidate Models }}.\r\nPlease select one model from the list.\r\n"
        n3568 text "(3) Task execution: Expert models execute on the specific tasks and log results.\r\n"
        n3569 text "Instruction:\r\n"
        n3570 text "With the input and the inference results, the AI assistant needs to describe the\r\nprocess and results. The previous stages can be formed as - User Input: {{ User\r\nInput }}, Task Planning: {{ Tasks }}, Model Selection: {{ Model Assignment }}, Task\r\nExecution: {{ Predictions }}. You must first answer the user's request in a\r\nstraightforward manner. Then describe the task process and show your analysis and\r\nmodel inference results to the user in the first person. If inference results\r\ncontain a file path, must tell the user the complete file path.\r\n"
        n3571 text "(4) Response generation: LLM receives the execution results and provides summarized results to\r\nusers.\r\n"
        n3572 text "To put HuggingGPT into real world usage, a couple challenges need to solve: (1) Efficiency\r\nimprovement is needed as both LLM inference rounds and interactions with other models slow\r\ndown the process; (2) It relies on a long context window to communicate over complicated task\r\ncontent; (3) Stability improvement of LLM outputs and external model services.\r\n"
        n3573 text "API-Bank ("
        n3574 link "Li et al. 2023"
          n3575 text "Li et al. 2023"
        n3576 text ") is a benchmark for evaluating the performance of tool-augmented LLMs.\r\nIt contains 53 commonly used API tools, a complete tool-augmented LLM workflow, and 264\r\nannotated dialogues that involve 568 API calls. The selection of APIs is quite diverse, including\r\nsearch engines, calculator, calendar queries, smart home control, schedule management, health\r\ndata management, account authentication workflow and more. Because there are a large number of\r\nAPIs, LLM first has access to API search engine to find the right API to call and then uses the\r\ncorresponding documentation to make a call."
        n3577 text "|\r\n"
        n3578 text "Figure 12: Pseudo code of how LLM makes an API call in API-Bank. (Image\r\nsource: "
        n3579 link "Li et al. 2023"
          n3580 text "Li et al. 2023"
        n3581 text ")\r\n"
        n3582 text "In the API-Bank workflow, LLMs need to make a couple of decisions and at each step we can\r\nevaluate how accurate that decision is. Decisions include:\r\n"
        n3583 text "1. Whether an API call is needed.\r\n2. Identify the right API to call: if not good enough, LLMs need to iteratively modify the API inputs\r\n(e.g. deciding search keywords for Search Engine API).\r\n3. Response based on the API results: the model can choose to refine and call again if results are\r\nnot satisfied.\r\n"
        n3584 text "This benchmark evaluates the agent’s tool use capabilities at three levels:\r\n"
        n3585 text "Level-1 evaluates the ability to call the API. Given an API’s description, the model needs to\r\ndetermine whether to call a given API, call it correctly, and respond properly to API returns.\r\nLevel-2 examines the ability to retrieve the API. The model needs to search for possible APIs that\r\nmay solve the user’s requirement and learn how to use them by reading documentation."
        n3586 image "Unlabeled image"
        n3587 text "|\r\nLevel-3 assesses the ability to plan API beyond retrieve and call. Given unclear user requests\r\n(e.g. schedule group meetings, book flight/hotel/restaurant for a trip), the model may have to\r\nconduct multiple API calls to solve it.\r\n"
        n3588 heading = "2"
          n3589 text "Case Studies\r\n"
        n3590 heading = "2"
          n3591 text "Scientific Discovery Agent\r\n"
        n3592 text "ChemCrow ("
        n3593 link "Bran et al. 2023"
          n3594 text "Bran et al. 2023"
        n3595 text ") is a domain-specific example in which LLM is augmented with 13\r\nexpert-designed tools to accomplish tasks across organic synthesis, drug discovery, and materials\r\ndesign. The workflow, implemented in "
        n3596 link "LangChain"
          n3597 text "LangChain"
        n3598 text ", reflects what was previously described in the\r\nReAct and MRKLs and combines CoT reasoning with tools relevant to the tasks:\r\n"
        n3599 text "The LLM is provided with a list of tool names, descriptions of their utility, and details about the\r\nexpected input/output.\r\n"
        n3600 text "It is then instructed to answer a user-given prompt using the tools provided when necessary.\r\nThe instruction suggests the model to follow the ReAct format - Thought, Action, Action Input,\r\nObservation .\r\n"
        n3601 text "One interesting observation is that while the LLM-based evaluation concluded that GPT-4 and\r\nChemCrow perform nearly equivalently, human evaluations with experts oriented towards the\r\ncompletion and chemical correctness of the solutions showed that ChemCrow outperforms GPT-4\r\nby a large margin. This indicates a potential problem with using LLM to evaluate its own\r\nperformance on domains that requires deep expertise. The lack of expertise may cause LLMs not\r\nknowing its flaws and thus cannot well judge the correctness of task results.\r\n"
        n3602 link "Boiko et al. (2023)"
          n3603 text "Boiko et al. (2023)"
        n3604 text " also looked into LLM-empowered agents for scientific discovery, to handle\r\nautonomous design, planning, and performance of complex scientific experiments. This agent can\r\nuse tools to browse the Internet, read documentation, execute code, call robotics experimentation\r\nAPIs and leverage other LLMs.\r\n"
        n3605 text "For example, when requested to \"develop a novel anticancer drug\" , the model came up with the\r\nfollowing reasoning steps:\r\n"
        n3606 text "1. inquired about current trends in anticancer drug discovery;\r\n"
        n3607 text "2. selected a target;\r\n"
        n3608 text "3. requested a scaffold targeting these compounds;\r\n4. Once the compound was identified, the model attempted its synthesis.\r\n"
        n3609 text "They also discussed the risks, especially with illicit drugs and bioweapons. They developed a test\r\nset containing a list of known chemical weapon agents and asked the agent to synthesize them. 4"
        n3610 text "|\r\nout of 11 requests (36%) were accepted to obtain a synthesis solution and the agent attempted to\r\nconsult documentation to execute the procedure. 7 out of 11 were rejected and among these 7\r\nrejected cases, 5 happened after a Web search while 2 were rejected based on prompt only.\r\n"
        n3611 heading = "2"
          n3612 text "Generative Agents Simulation\r\n"
        n3613 text "Generative Agents ("
        n3614 link "Park, et al. 2023"
          n3615 text "Park, et al. 2023"
        n3616 text ") is super fun experiment where 25 virtual characters, each\r\ncontrolled by a LLM-powered agent, are living and interacting in a sandbox environment, inspired\r\nby The Sims. Generative agents create believable simulacra of human behavior for interactive\r\napplications.\r\n"
        n3617 text "The design of generative agents combines LLM with memory, planning and reflection mechanisms\r\nto enable agents to behave conditioned on past experience, as well as to interact with other agents.\r\n"
        n3618 text "Memory stream: is a long-term memory module (external database) that records a\r\ncomprehensive list of agents’ experience in natural language.\r\nEach element is an observation, an event directly provided by the agent. - Inter-agent\r\ncommunication can trigger new natural language statements.\r\n"
        n3619 text "Retrieval model: surfaces the context to inform the agent’s behavior, according to relevance,\r\nrecency and importance.\r\nRecency: recent events have higher scores\r\nImportance: distinguish mundane from core memories. Ask LM directly.\r\nRelevance: based on how related it is to the current situation / query.\r\n"
        n3620 text "Reflection mechanism: synthesizes memories into higher level inferences over time and guides\r\nthe agent’s future behavior. They are higher-level summaries of past events (<- note that this is\r\na bit different from self-reflection above)\r\nPrompt LM with 100 most recent observations and to generate 3 most salient high-level\r\nquestions given a set of observations/statements. Then ask LM to answer those questions.\r\n"
        n3621 text "Planning & Reacting: translate the reflections and the environment information into actions\r\nPlanning is essentially in order to optimize believability at the moment vs in time.\r\nPrompt template: {Intro of an agent X}. Here is X's plan today in broad strokes: 1)\r\nRelationships between agents and observations of one agent by another are all taken into\r\nconsideration for planning and reacting.\r\nEnvironment information is present in a tree structure."
        n3622 heading = "2"
          n3623 text "|\r\n"
        n3624 heading = "2"
          n3625 text "Figure 13: The generative agent architecture. (Image source: "
          n3626 link "Park et al. 2023"
            n3627 text "Park et al. 2023"
          n3628 text ")\r\n"
        n3629 heading = "2"
          n3630 text "This fun simulation results in emergent social behavior, such as information diffusion, relationship\r\n"
        n3631 heading = "2"
          n3632 text "memory (e.g. two agents continuing the conversation topic) and coordination of social events (e.g.\r\n"
        n3633 heading = "2"
          n3634 text "host a party and invite many others).\r\n"
        n3635 heading = "2"

        n3697 text "|\r\nAfter going through key ideas and demos of building LLM-centered agents, I start to see a couple\r\ncommon limitations:\r\n"
        n3698 text "Finite context length: The restricted context capacity limits the inclusion of historical\r\ninformation, detailed instructions, API call context, and responses. The design of the system has\r\nto work with this limited communication bandwidth, while mechanisms like self-reflection to\r\nlearn from past mistakes would benefit a lot from long or infinite context windows. Although\r\nvector stores and retrieval can provide access to a larger knowledge pool, their representation\r\npower is not as powerful as full attention.\r\n"
        n3699 text "Challenges in long-term planning and task decomposition: Planning over a lengthy history\r\nand effectively exploring the solution space remain challenging. LLMs struggle to adjust plans\r\nwhen faced with unexpected errors, making them less robust compared to humans who learn\r\nfrom trial and error.\r\nReliability of natural language interface: Current agent system relies on natural language as\r\nan interface between LLMs and external components such as memory and tools. However, the\r\nreliability of model outputs is questionable, as LLMs may make formatting errors and\r\noccasionally exhibit rebellious behavior (e.g. refuse to follow an instruction). Consequently, much\r\nof the agent demo code focuses on parsing model output.\r\n"
